Forest: Forest shows a continuous canopy of dense tree cover with very little exposed soil or pavement.
Forest appears as irregular dark green masses rather than the straight-edged plots typical of cropland.
Forest has a coarse, bumpy texture from tree crowns instead of the smooth uniform surface of grassland.
Forest usually contains winding narrow clearings or tracks rather than a regular street grid.
Forest forms large uninterrupted blocks of vegetation with sparse or absent buildings.
Forest has uneven natural boundaries that follow terrain or waterways instead of geometric parcel lines.
Forest often includes scattered shadows and tonal variation created by tall vegetation across the canopy.
Forest is dominated by deep green to olive tones rather than the tan or bright green patches of cultivated fields.
Forest may contain small dark streams or ponds embedded within dense tree cover.
Forest lacks the repeated roof patterns and compact building clusters seen in residential or industrial areas.
Forest shows a mottled texture with many individual crown-sized spots visible from above.
Forest has branching access roads that terminate within tree cover instead of connecting many dense structures.
Forest often covers slopes and ridges as contiguous vegetation where urban land would break into blocks.
Forest contains few sharp corners in land cover patterns compared with the rectangular outlines of managed land.
Forest presents a layered canopy appearance with mixed light and dark patches rather than a flat monochrome surface.
Forest has minimal bare ground, with openings appearing as small irregular gaps within the trees.
Forest appears more continuous and darker than shrubland, with less visible spacing between plants.
Forest shows natural sinuous edges along rivers or lakes bordered by dense vegetation.
Forest lacks the linear row patterns that orchards or plantations often display from above.
Forest is characterized by broad expanses of textured tree cover broken only occasionally by thin roads or clearings.
Highway or Road: Highway or Road appears as a long, narrow linear corridor cutting across the landscape with strong directional continuity.
Highway or Road shows smooth, paved strips in gray or dark tones that contrast with surrounding vegetation or bare soil.
Highway or Road often forms branching or intersecting line networks rather than the blocky building clusters of residential areas.
Highway or Road is characterized by elongated geometry with a very high length-to-width ratio compared with runways or parking lots.
Highway or Road may include parallel lanes separated by a thin median, creating a paired-line pattern from above.
Highway or Road frequently curves gently across hills or plains instead of forming the rigid rectangular parcels seen in cropland.
Highway or Road has sparse built structures directly on the corridor, unlike industrial or commercial zones with large roof footprints.
Highway or Road commonly connects scattered urban patches while remaining itself a mostly continuous impervious strip.
Highway or Road can appear as interchanges with looping ramps and arcs, producing knot-like junction patterns.
Highway or Road usually occupies only a small fraction of the scene width while traversing much of the scene length.
Highway or Road is bordered by thin shoulders or cleared edges that create crisp boundaries against adjacent land cover.
Highway or Road often crosses rivers or fields as uninterrupted lines, unlike waterways that show irregular banks and variable width.
Highway or Road may be accompanied by service roads, creating multiple closely spaced parallel lines.
Highway or Road lacks the dense fine texture of tree canopy and instead presents a smooth uniform surface texture.
Highway or Road in urban settings appears as a dominant linear spine with feeder streets extending outward in smaller branches.
Highway or Road commonly slices through forests or farmland, dividing large land-cover patches into separated sections.
Highway or Road has a consistent engineered width over long distances, unlike natural channels that widen and narrow irregularly.
Highway or Road may include central barriers or lane markings that give a faint striped appearance along the corridor.
Highway or Road is often surrounded by narrow roadside grass strips rather than the broad open paved expanses of airports.
Highway or Road stands out by its connected transportation geometry, not by isolated rectangular roofs, circular tanks, or field grids.
Residential Buildings: Residential Buildings shows many small to medium rooftops packed closely together in a continuous built-up area.
Residential Buildings has a dense street grid or curving neighborhood roads lined with repeated house-sized structures.
Residential Buildings contains numerous individual building footprints separated by small gaps rather than large industrial sheds.
Residential Buildings often appears as clusters of homes mixed with small yards and patches of green vegetation.
Residential Buildings has a finer-grained texture than commercial or industrial areas because the buildings are smaller and more numerous.
Residential Buildings usually lacks the large uniform paved expanses that surround warehouses, factories, or airports.
Residential Buildings often forms subdivisions with looping streets, cul-de-sacs, and evenly spaced lots.
Residential Buildings shows a mottled pattern of gray roofs, light pavement, and scattered green tree cover.
Residential Buildings includes narrow local streets that branch frequently, unlike the wide straight corridors of major transport zones.
Residential Buildings commonly has rectangular or irregular housing plots that repeat across the neighborhood.
Residential Buildings presents moderate to high building density but still includes visible gardens, lawns, or tree canopies between structures.
Residential Buildings has a more organized neighborhood pattern than informal settlements, with clearer lot boundaries and road alignment.
Residential Buildings typically contains many detached or attached units rather than a few very large building blocks.
Residential Buildings often transitions gradually into parks, schools, or small open spaces instead of expansive crop fields.
Residential Buildings shows compact blocks of houses with roofs of similar size and spacing across the area.
Residential Buildings usually has less bare soil than construction sites and less continuous vegetation than forests or farmland.
Residential Buildings may include apartment complexes that appear as repeated mid-sized blocks arranged along internal access roads.
Residential Buildings has an overall patchwork appearance created by rooftops, driveways, sidewalks, and small vegetation pockets.
Residential Buildings often follows a neighborhood layout with intersecting residential streets rather than isolated buildings in open land.
Residential Buildings is characterized by built surfaces dominating the scene while vegetation remains fragmented into small residential patches.
Pasture Land: Pasture Land shows broad open grass-covered areas in light green to yellow-green tones with very few dense tree canopies.
Pasture Land often appears as large irregular or gently rectangular fields separated by thin fences, hedgerows, or narrow tracks.
Pasture Land has a smoother, more uniform vegetation texture than forested classes, without a continuous dark rough canopy.
Pasture Land usually contains sparse, scattered trees or small tree clusters rather than dense woodland blocks.
Pasture Land is dominated by open fields with low building density, unlike residential or industrial areas with tightly grouped structures.
Pasture Land often lacks the repetitive row patterns seen in orchards or plantations, showing instead continuous grassy surfaces.
Pasture Land commonly forms a patchwork of medium to large parcels with soft boundaries rather than many tiny fragmented plots.
Pasture Land has a subdued green-brown color palette that is more natural and less bare than construction or mining land.
Pasture Land may include winding farm tracks or minor roads, but it does not show a dense urban street grid.
Pasture Land frequently borders small ponds or narrow streams embedded within open grassy parcels.
Pasture Land presents field interiors that are mostly clear and open, with little internal shadow compared with wooded land.
Pasture Land often appears less geometrically precise than cropland, with parcels that follow rolling terrain or natural edges.
Pasture Land can show faint boundary lines and enclosure patterns without the strong linear planting marks of cultivated fields.
Pasture Land has a relatively even surface tone across each field, without the strong alternating bands typical of harvested cropland.
Pasture Land usually includes isolated farm buildings spaced far apart, not compact clusters of rooftops.
Pasture Land may contain narrow riparian tree lines tracing drainage paths through otherwise open grassland.
Pasture Land shows more continuous vegetation cover than barren land, but the cover is lower and lighter than forest.
Pasture Land often transitions gradually between green and dry beige patches, creating a mottled but still open appearance.
Pasture Land lacks the bright reflective surfaces and paved expanses associated with commercial or transportation classes.
Pasture Land is characterized by expansive open enclosures where vegetation dominates and built structures occupy only a very small fraction of the area.
River: River appears as a long, continuous ribbon of water winding across the landscape.
River has a smooth dark blue or brown surface that contrasts with the surrounding land.
River is narrow and elongated rather than forming the broad open shape of a lake or reservoir.
River often shows sinuous meanders and looping bends instead of straight field boundaries.
River is bordered by linear strips of dense green vegetation tracing both banks.
River cuts through the scene as a branching channel network with occasional tributaries joining in.
River has irregular natural edges rather than the sharp geometric outlines of canals or ponds.
River may contain sandbars or small islands as pale patches within the watercourse.
River separates adjacent land parcels with an organic curving corridor across farmland or forest.
River usually lacks the dense building coverage seen in urban classes, leaving a mostly open water corridor.
River can appear braided in places, with multiple shallow channels spread across a wider bed.
River often includes floodplain areas of lighter sediment or moist vegetation alongside the main channel.
River crosses roads at isolated bridge points rather than being enclosed by a street grid.
River forms a connected path through the entire scene instead of isolated water patches.
River shows a variable width along its course, widening and narrowing naturally over distance.
River creates strong contrast between the dark water channel and bright exposed banks or sediment.
River follows a natural curving route that ignores the rectangular geometry of agricultural plots.
River may have oxbow-shaped curves or cutoff loops along nearby low-lying land.
River is commonly lined by trees in a narrow continuous band, unlike open grassland or bare soil.
River dominates the scene with a directional water corridor rather than scattered buildings or uniform vegetation.
Sea or Lake: Sea or Lake is dominated by a broad continuous water surface with almost no built structures interrupting it.
Sea or Lake appears as a large dark blue, gray, or black area with smooth tonal variation rather than the textured patterns of vegetation.
Sea or Lake has an irregular shoreline that separates open water from adjacent land in a clear curving boundary.
Sea or Lake lacks the rectangular field grids and parcel lines typical of agricultural land.
Sea or Lake shows no dense street network or compact building blocks like urban or industrial areas.
Sea or Lake often contains gentle wave-like ripples or subtle streaks across the surface instead of land texture.
Sea or Lake includes coves, bays, or peninsulas where land protrudes into the water in rounded shapes.
Sea or Lake may contain small islands appearing as isolated land patches surrounded on all sides by water.
Sea or Lake has a mostly uniform surface color that contrasts with the mottled greens of forested land.
Sea or Lake is much more open and uninterrupted than river corridors, which are narrow and elongated.
Sea or Lake may have bright shallow edges near the shore where the water color lightens gradually.
Sea or Lake contains very few linear transport features, except occasional bridges or causeways crossing the water.
Sea or Lake shows wide expanses without the scattered rooftops or village clusters seen in settled land.
Sea or Lake forms a single connected water body rather than many small ponds fragmented across the landscape.
Sea or Lake has smooth natural outlines rather than the sharp engineered edges common in ports or reservoirs with embankments.
Sea or Lake is bordered in places by beaches, marshy margins, or rocky coasts that create thin edge textures around the water.
Sea or Lake occupies a large contiguous area that overwhelms nearby land cover in the scene.
Sea or Lake has no visible crop rows, orchard dots, or plantation striping anywhere across its main surface.
Sea or Lake may show tonal bands from wind or depth changes, but not the branching canopy texture of wetlands.
Sea or Lake is characterized by open water extending to the scene edge, unlike enclosed recreational or residential water features.
Industrial Buildings: Industrial Buildings shows large rectangular roof blocks clustered on paved lots.
Industrial Buildings has wide warehouse-like structures arranged in regular rows with clear spacing between them.
Industrial Buildings contains a high proportion of gray and white rooftops compared with surrounding vegetation.
Industrial Buildings is dominated by impervious surfaces such as concrete yards and access roads rather than crop patterns.
Industrial Buildings features broad service roads and turning areas forming a coarse internal street layout.
Industrial Buildings often appears as fenced compounds of big buildings separated from nearby residential street grids.
Industrial Buildings includes long linear roofs and loading-side aprons that create strong parallel edges from above.
Industrial Buildings has sparse tree cover, with vegetation limited to narrow strips along parcel boundaries.
Industrial Buildings forms large contiguous developed parcels, unlike the finer mix of houses and gardens in urban residential areas.
Industrial Buildings shows blocky building footprints much larger than typical commercial or residential structures.
Industrial Buildings has a muted palette of light gray roofs, dark asphalt, and small patches of dull green.
Industrial Buildings often sits beside rail spurs or very wide roads, creating elongated transport corridors next to the buildings.
Industrial Buildings displays low building density in count but very high roof-area coverage because each structure is expansive.
Industrial Buildings has roofs with varied industrial textures such as vents and segmented panels visible as fine rooftop patterns.
Industrial Buildings lacks the circular tanks and highly reflective surfaces that distinguish many refinery or utility sites.
Industrial Buildings presents rectangular plots with straight property lines and minimal curving road geometry.
Industrial Buildings usually has few or no water bodies inside the complex, with paved open space dominating the gaps.
Industrial Buildings shows detached buildings aligned to parcel edges rather than tightly packed continuous urban blocks.
Industrial Buildings often includes open storage yards as bare or paved rectangles adjacent to the main structures.
Industrial Buildings appears more orderly and geometric than construction sites, with completed roofs and stable surface patterns.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land: Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows broad continuous cover of low green vegetation without dense tree canopy from above.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land appears as a soft, fine-grained texture that is smoother than forest and rougher than bare soil.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land is dominated by green to yellow-green tones rather than the dark green of wooded areas.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land usually lacks the tight rectangular field boundaries seen in intensively cultivated cropland.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land forms open patches with irregular natural edges instead of compact urban blocks.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has very sparse buildings, with large vegetated gaps between any structures.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows few roads, and any tracks are thin and loosely connected rather than gridlike.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land often appears as expansive open ground with scattered tonal variation but no strong row patterns.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks the circular crowns or shadow patterns that mark orchards or tree plantations.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land presents a relatively even surface cover without the bright exposed mineral patches of barren land.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land may include narrow meandering drainage lines, but water does not dominate the scene.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has a mottled grassy texture that is more continuous than scrubland with isolated bushes.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land usually shows weak parcel geometry, with boundaries that are faint, curved, or absent.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land appears flatter in texture than wetlands with dense reed mosaics and open water pockets.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land commonly covers large uninterrupted areas with little contrast from one patch to the next.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows seasonal color variation within a grassy palette, from pale straw to fresh green.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land does not display the repeated parallel planting lines typical of managed crop fields.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has an open landscape pattern where vegetation cover dominates over pavement and rooftops.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land often transitions gradually into shrub or forest edges rather than ending at sharp artificial borders.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land appears as non-woody vegetated terrain with low vertical structure and minimal shadowing.
Annual Crop Land: Annual Crop Land shows a patchwork of medium to large rectangular fields with crisp parcel boundaries.
Annual Crop Land contains mostly open cultivated plots with very few dense tree crowns interrupting the fields.
Annual Crop Land has a regular agricultural grid broken by straight field-edge roads and drainage lines.
Annual Crop Land appears in alternating tan, brown, and green blocks that change from plot to plot.
Annual Crop Land is dominated by bare soil or low vegetation textures rather than the continuous rough canopy of forest.
Annual Crop Land has broad uniform fields that are larger and less fragmented than typical mixed residential areas.
Annual Crop Land often forms expansive contiguous tracts of farmland with sparse scattered farm buildings only.
Annual Crop Land shows sharp geometric edges between plots instead of the irregular boundaries common in natural vegetation.
Annual Crop Land has a smoother, lower-texture surface than orchards, lacking dense rows of evenly spaced tree dots.
Annual Crop Land includes straight or gently curving access roads that divide fields without forming an urban street grid.
Annual Crop Land usually lacks large industrial roofs, with land cover dominated by cultivated ground instead of built surfaces.
Annual Crop Land may contain narrow irrigation or drainage channels, but water occupies only a small fraction of the scene.
Annual Crop Land presents repeated field parcels with different tones, creating a checkerboard or striped agricultural pattern.
Annual Crop Land has minimal shadowing because most of the area is flat and covered by low crops or exposed soil.
Annual Crop Land is less uniformly green than permanent pasture, with many plots appearing brown or freshly worked.
Annual Crop Land shows strong seasonal contrast between neighboring parcels, with some fields bright green and others pale or dark earth.
Annual Crop Land has sparse settlement presence, with buildings appearing isolated rather than clustered into villages or suburbs.
Annual Crop Land often includes long straight plot boundaries aligned in parallel, emphasizing a surveyed agricultural layout.
Annual Crop Land is characterized by open land cover continuity, without the dense impervious surfaces of commercial or urban classes.
Annual Crop Land shows field-scale geometry as the main visual structure, with vegetation arranged by parcels rather than by natural patches.
Permanent Crop Land: Permanent Crop Land shows dense vegetation arranged in regular rows or grids across many small to medium plots.
Permanent Crop Land contains orchards or plantations with evenly spaced tree or shrub crowns forming a dotted pattern from above.
Permanent Crop Land has a more repetitive planting texture than mixed annual cropland, with the same row spacing continuing across each plot.
Permanent Crop Land often appears as compact blocks of dark green vegetation broken by narrow service tracks.
Permanent Crop Land shows field parcels with clear boundaries but interiors filled by uniform perennial cover rather than bare soil patches.
Permanent Crop Land has a striped or ribbed surface texture caused by parallel planting lines visible across the fields.
Permanent Crop Land presents a consistent green to deep green palette over large areas, with less seasonal color contrast than harvested arable land.
Permanent Crop Land includes many rectangular or gently curving plots whose internal vegetation pattern is more regular than natural forest.
Permanent Crop Land shows scattered farm buildings only occasionally, with vegetation dominating far more area than built structures.
Permanent Crop Land has a finer, more ordered texture than shrubland, lacking the random patchiness of wild vegetation.
Permanent Crop Land often follows gentle terrain with contour-aligned rows that create smooth, parallel bands across slopes.
Permanent Crop Land displays repeated circular or rounded canopy dots in neat spacing, unlike the continuous canopy of woodland.
Permanent Crop Land is crossed by a sparse network of straight or lightly curving access paths separating planted blocks.
Permanent Crop Land usually lacks the wide paved street grid of urban areas, with roads serving mainly to divide agricultural parcels.
Permanent Crop Land shows little open water, and if channels are present they are narrow lines beside cultivated plots.
Permanent Crop Land has more permanent woody cover inside fields than pasture, which appears smoother and less geometrically planted.
Permanent Crop Land forms mosaics of cultivated blocks where each block has a highly uniform internal pattern distinct from neighboring blocks.
Permanent Crop Land often has plot shapes that are elongated and aligned, emphasizing the direction of planting rows.
Permanent Crop Land appears less fragmented by houses than rural residential land, with large uninterrupted planted sections.
Permanent Crop Land shows a deliberate agricultural geometry superimposed on the landscape, combining regular parcel outlines with persistent vegetation cover.
